home.heroTitle: One in six of your visitors can't use your website.
home.heroSubtitle: Roughly 1.3 billion people live with a disability. Yet the 2024 WebAIM study found 96% of the web's most-visited pages fail basic accessibility checks. Enter your address and we'll show you — in plain words — which of those failures are on your site, and exactly what to fix. Free, forever.
home.differenceBody: Most scanners find the obvious faults, then shrug at the rest. That's not good enough, because 69% of disabled users simply leave a site they can't use. We don't leave. Machines catch what machines can; AI-assisted review covers the rest; and independent human reviewers — people with lived experience of disability — will confirm what neither can, producing a signed, evidence-backed report rather than a shrug.
home.step2Body: We assess it, free, against WCAG — the international standard.
home.step3Body: You get the top issues to fix first, with the fix and the proof.
home.sampleNote: An example report. Yours shows a score, the top issues to fix first, and how each was tested — machine, AI, or human review.
home.sampleIssue2: Text color contrast is too low
home.persona1Body: Government teams — evidence for the WCAG AA your citizens are owed.
home.persona2Body: NGOs — every person you serve deserves to be served.
home.persona3Body: Funders — verifiable proof, not a promise.
home.persona4Body: Developers — the exact issue, the fix, the element.
home.outcome1Body: WCAG 2.0, 2.1, 2.2 (A/AA/AAA) and Section 508, mapped to EN 301 549 and regional regulations.
home.outcome2Body: Every finding carries the affected element, page, and WCAG reference — an auditable record.
home.outcome3Body: Certified reviewers with lived experience of disability — paid on a cost-recovery basis — resolve what automation cannot.
home.outcome4Title: A report you can act on
home.outcome4Body: Signed, dated, and ranked by what to fix first — with a suggested fix for each issue.
home.trustPoint1: Independent human review, built with disability-serving charities — coming soon.
home.trustPoint2: Free — funded by donations, not by charging you.
home.trustPoint3: We hold ourselves to the same bar: this site targets WCAG 2.2 AAA.
home.trustPoint4: Open source — our engines are public, so you can see exactly how we test.
home.founderBody1: Simon Mak is an entrepreneur, author, and sustainability advocate — and he lives with Parkinson's disease. He founded Ascent Partners Foundation because accessibility is not an abstract cause to him; it is personal. That is why this tool is built by people with lived experience of disability — from our founder to the review workforce we are building with disability-serving charities — for everyone who is too often excluded from the web.
home.founderBody2: His work connects finance and sustainability — and digital accessibility is the "social" in ESG.

about.title: About Ascent Partners Foundation
about.description: Ascent Partners Foundation is a Hong Kong registered charity connecting leaders with the tools to turn sustainability into action.
about.heading: About Ascent Partners Foundation
about.intro: In 2017, a Hong Kong charity asked a simple question: what if the leaders who talk about sustainability had the tools to actually practise it? Ascent Partners Foundation was the answer. We are a registered charity (IRD Section 88) connecting government, civil society, and the private sector across the Asia-Pacific — because the "S" in ESG is not a spreadsheet cell. It is whether a real person can use what you built.
about.charityNote: A Hong Kong Registered Charity (IRD Section 88).
about.focus1Body: supporting climate dialogue, nature-based solutions, and decarbonization pathways.
about.focus2Body: educational resources and guidance on environmental, social, and governance principles for businesses and practitioners.
about.focus3Body: an IUCN partnership connecting conservation initiatives with philanthropic communities, and professional conservation education.
about.toolsTitle: Why we built a free accessibility tool
about.toolsBody: Inclusion is the easiest word to write and the hardest to measure. So we built a way to measure it. Type a web address and our free tool — with its open-source assessment and AI engines — tells you whether that site welcomes everyone, in words any leader can act on. It is a starting point, not a verdict.
about.peopleBody: We are a small, caring team, and we welcome people who share this mission — whether you would like help with your own site, want to contribute your expertise, or are interested in joining us. Please say hello.

humanReviewPage.title: Human review — coming soon
humanReviewPage.description: Independent human review is coming soon. We are building a review workforce in partnership with charities that serve people with visual and hearing disabilities — lived-experience experts who will verify what automation cannot.
humanReviewPage.heading: Independent human review
humanReviewPage.intro: A scanner can tell you an image is missing its description. It cannot tell you the description is wrong. That gap — between what a machine detects and what a person understands — is why human review exists. We are building a workforce of people with lived experience of disability to close it, in partnership with the charities that serve them.
humanReviewPage.whyBody: There is a reason lived experience cannot be automated. A reviewer who navigates with a screen reader notices in seconds what a checklist misses — focus order that doesn't match reading order, alt text that describes the wrong thing, a form error that is announced but not actionable. That judgement turns a score into an assurance you can defend. And it will be paid work: the insight is the product, billed per page on a cost-recovery basis — never for profit. Every reviewer is certified through the Ascent Web Accessibility Program.
humanReviewPage.whatBody: Every criterion the engine and AI cannot decide is flagged "Cannot tell". When human review launches, a reviewer whose own experience matches the barrier will resolve each one — Passed, Failed, or Not present — with a written rationale, against the exact page snapshot captured at assessment time. So the result is reproducible, even if the live site changes.
humanReviewPage.receiveBody: A signed, dated <link>conformance evaluation report</link>, structured like an assurance engagement: scope, evaluators, review process, per-criterion results, a conformance claim, and key findings — in-app and as a PDF, with a VPAT/ACR export for procurement.
humanReviewPage.meantimeBody: You can already run a free assessment and get a partial, automated result — clearly marked as such — with a suggested fix for each issue. Independent human review completes the picture when it launches.

forGovernment.title: For government
forGovernment.description: Independent accessibility verification for government digital and policy teams — meet WCAG AA mandates with evidence, not just a self-declared statement. Free to start.
forGovernment.heading: Accessibility assurance for government
forGovernment.intro: Here is an uncomfortable statistic for any public servant: when the UK's Fable study asked disabled users what they do on an inaccessible website, 69% said they simply leave. For a government, a citizen who "leaves" is a service not delivered — a right not met. This page is for the teams whose job is to make sure that never happens.
forGovernment.requirementBody: The standard behind Hong Kong's digital-government guidelines, America's Section 508, Europe's EN 301 549, and the European Accessibility Act is WCAG Level AA. In plain terms: public information must reach every citizen, whatever their disability.
forGovernment.selfDeclaredTitle: Why a self-declared statement is not enough
forGovernment.selfDeclaredBody: Anyone can publish a statement that says "we're compliant". What survives scrutiny is evidence — a signed, dated report showing exactly which criteria pass, which fail, and which needed a human eye, with the proof attached. That is what auditors, ombudsmen, and procurement teams ask for.
forGovernment.getItem1Body: automated assessing across WCAG 2.0, 2.1, 2.2 and Section 508, mapped to EN 301 549.
forGovernment.getItem2Body: the top issues to fix first, each with a suggested fix and the evidence.
forGovernment.getItem3Body: people with lived experience of disability will confirm what automation cannot.
forGovernment.getItem4Body: an auditable record for governance, procurement, and public accountability.
forGovernment.trustBody: We hold ourselves to the same standard — this site targets WCAG 2.2 AAA. Our method is open (<methodology>methodology</methodology>) and our engine is documented (<validation>how we validate it</validation>). Human review (launching soon) will be done by paid, certified experts with lived experience of disability, on a cost-recovery basis — not a token check.

forNgos.title: For NGOs
forNgos.description: Free website accessibility checking for NGOs and community services — reach every person you serve, including people with disabilities. Free forever, no expertise needed.
forNgos.heading: Accessibility for NGOs and community services
forNgos.intro: The people your charity exists to help are often the people an inaccessible website locks out first. If your page can't be read by a screen reader, navigated by keyboard, or understood by everyone, then the people who need you most are the ones turned away. Accessibility is how you make sure no one is left out.
forNgos.missionBody: The people you exist to help are often the people most affected by an inaccessible website. If someone cannot read your page with a screen reader, navigate it by keyboard, or understand your forms, they are cut off from your service. Accessibility is how you make sure no one is left out.
forNgos.freeTitle: Free forever — built for non-profit budgets
forNgos.freeBody: Assessing is free — always. We are a registered charity funded by donations, not by charging you. There is no paywall and no trial that expires.
forNgos.evidenceBody: Digital inclusion is part of the "social" in ESG. A clear accessibility report shows funders and grant assessors that you take inclusion seriously — with evidence, not just intention. <link>See how it maps to GRI, ESRS, and SASB</link>.
forNgos.getItem1Body: a score and the top issues to fix first, in words anyone can follow.
forNgos.getItem2Body: for each issue, with the evidence.

That's the honest version: there is no trial, no paywall, and no "premium tier", because Ascent Accessibility is not a software subscription. It is a free, open-source tool built by a registered charity, funded by donations and — soon — cost-recovery human review. Here is the whole model, in plain words.

plans.free3: Conformance outcome with 'x of y applicable SCs meet'
plans.free4: Findings with impact, affected elements, and pages
plans.free5: Plain-language remediation guidance for every finding

plans.byok2: Bring your own key for OpenRouter, OpenAI, Qwen, Gemini, or Anthropic — or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint
plans.byok3: Fail-safe: nothing is marked passed without high confidence
plans.byok4: Covered by your existing key; no per-assessment fee

primer.title: What is web accessibility?
primer.description: A plain-language introduction to web accessibility for NGOs and government — what it means, who it affects, why it matters, and how to start. No jargon.
primer.heading: What is web accessibility?
primer.intro: There is a door you walk through every day without noticing. It opens for you. Now imagine it doesn't. For one in six people, much of the web is that door. This is the two-minute explanation of why — and what "accessible" actually means.
primer.shortBody1: It means your website works for everyone — including the one in six people living with a disability. A person who is blind, has low vision, cannot hear, has limited movement, or finds dense text hard to follow should still be able to read, navigate, and use what you publish.
primer.shortBody2: It is not a special feature for a few people. It is simply a website that works for everyone.
primer.whoBody1: One in six people live with a disability — the single most important number in this field. And disability is wider than you think: it can be permanent (blindness), temporary (a broken arm), or situational (bright sunlight on a phone screen, or holding a baby).
primer.whoBody2: Design for disability and you usually make things better for everyone — the ramp helps the wheelchair user, and also the parent with a pram.
primer.whyItem1Body: You serve your whole community, not just part of it.
primer.whyItem2Body: Everyone deserves equal access to public information and services.
primer.whyItem3Body: Many governments and funders ask for it by law or policy.
primer.pourIntro: WCAG — the web accessibility standard — groups everything into four principles:
primer.pour1Body: People can see or hear it — images carry text alternatives, so nothing is lost on a screen reader.
primer.pour2Body: People can use it — everything works with a keyboard, not just a mouse.
primer.pour3Body: People can follow it — clear language, predictable behaviour.
primer.pour4Body: It keeps working as the tools evolve, now and in the future.
primer.toolsBody: People browse the web in many ways: a screen reader that reads the page aloud, screen magnification, keyboard-only navigation, voice control, or a switch device. A good website works with all of them — not just the ones you happened to test.
primer.standardBody: WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) is the international standard — the numbers from the World Health Organization and the world's accessibility laws all point back to it. It has three levels: A, AA, and AAA. Most laws and policies ask for AA; this site itself targets AAA, the highest. <link1>Browse the WCAG criteria</link1> or look up any term in our <link2>plain-language glossary</link2>.
primer.startBody: You do not need to be an expert. Run a free assessment of your site to see where you stand, or take the free course to learn at your own pace.

methodology.title: Methodology
methodology.description: How Ascent Accessibility scores a website — crawling, the Ascent Accessibility engine, site audit signals, and the scoring model.
methodology.heading: Methodology
methodology.intro: A score is only as trustworthy as the method behind it. Here, in full, is how we get from a web address to a verdict — so you can judge the tool, not just the number.
methodology.crawlBody: Whole-website assessments start with the site's sitemap.xml, falling back to a link crawl, and respect robots.txt. Crawling is bounded by a depth and a page cap, so very large sites may be reported as covering a subset of pages.
methodology.scanBody: Each page is assessed with the Ascent Accessibility engine — an in-house, clean-room, open-source WCAG rule engine — against the rules for the standard you selected. Automated rules detect only issues that can be identified automatically, roughly 30–50% of WCAG criteria. A companion site audit measures performance, SEO, and best-practice signals, and an optional AI-assisted review narrows the items that require manual judgement.
methodology.scoreBody: The score starts at 100 and subtracts a fixed weight per finding — critical −10, serious −5, moderate −2, minor −0.5 — capped per finding. 90+ is a pass, 70–89 is partial, and below 70 is a fail. The conformance table separately tracks which success criteria pass, fail, are not applicable, or need manual review.
methodology.limitsBody: Automated tools cannot judge meaning, so many criteria (for example, whether alt text is accurate, or whether content is genuinely understandable) require human review. A clean score is encouraging, but it is not a certificate of conformance. Treat the report as a starting point for a manual review.
methodology.seeAll: See the full list of <link>WCAG 2.2 success criteria</link> the tool scores against.
methodology.whoReviewsBody: Criteria the engine and AI cannot determine are resolved by a certified reviewer with lived experience of the barrier they affect. Every reviewer is certified through the Ascent Web Accessibility Program.
methodology.validationBody: Our engine is clean-room and open source — built from the W3C's own success criteria and the ACT-rules format, not from any third-party scanner. That means every rule can be inspected, and the engine benchmarked against the W3C/WAI test suites. We publish the method precisely so the evidence behind your report is verifiable.

glossary.heading: Accessibility glossary
glossary.description: Plain-language definitions of web accessibility and WCAG terms — written for non-experts in NGOs and government. What each term means and why it matters.
glossary.intro: Plain-language definitions of the terms this site — and the accessibility field — use constantly. Each one says what it means and why it matters. No jargon. New to accessibility? Start with our <link>plain-language introduction</link>.

accessibility.definition: Websites and apps that everyone can use, including people with disabilities.
accessibility.why: Accessibility removes barriers so no one is locked out.

wcag.definition: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines — the international standard for web accessibility.
wcag.why: It is the rulebook most accessibility laws and policies point to.

successCriterion.definition: A single, testable rule in WCAG, such as “images must have a text alternative”.
successCriterion.why: Each one is a specific thing you can check on a page.

pour.definition: The four principles WCAG is built on: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust.
pour.why: It is a simple way to group every rule in the standard.

levels.definition: The three levels of WCAG conformance, from basic (A) to highest (AAA).
levels.why: Most laws and policies ask for level AA. This site itself targets AAA.

altText.definition: A short written description of an image, read aloud by screen readers.
altText.why: It tells people who cannot see the image what it shows.

screenReader.definition: Software that reads the screen aloud for people who are blind or have low vision.
screenReader.why: It is one of the main tools people use to browse the web.

assistiveTechnology.definition: Any tool that helps a person with a disability use the web — a screen reader, magnifier, switch device, or voice control.
assistiveTechnology.why: Good websites work with these tools, not against them.

keyboardAccessible.definition: Everything on the page can be used with a keyboard alone — no mouse needed.
keyboardAccessible.why: Many people navigate by keyboard, switch device, or voice control.

focusIndicator.definition: The visible outline that shows where you are on the page when using a keyboard.
focusIndicator.why: Without it, keyboard users get lost.

colourContrast.definition: A measure of how different the text color is from its background.
colourContrast.why: Low contrast makes text hard to read, especially for people with low vision.

landmark.definition: A labeled region of a page, such as the header, navigation, or main content.
landmark.why: Screen-reader users jump between landmarks to find things fast.

headingStructure.definition: Using real headings (h1, h2, h3) in the right order to outline the page.
headingStructure.why: It is how screen-reader users skim and navigate.

aria.definition: A set of HTML attributes that add accessibility information to custom controls.
aria.why: Used carefully it fills gaps HTML alone cannot — but native HTML always comes first.

conformance.definition: How well a site meets WCAG — whether it passes, fails, or needs human review.
conformance.why: It is the honest measure of where your site stands.

automatedTest.definition: A check run by software, with no human judgement.
automatedTest.why: Fast and consistent, but it can only catch part of the picture.

manualTest.definition: A check done by a person, such as testing with a keyboard or a screen reader.
manualTest.why: Some things only a human can judge.

aiAssistedReview.definition: Using AI to help check the things automation alone cannot decide.
aiAssistedReview.why: It narrows the gap, but a person still confirms the result — it is not proof.

vpat.definition: A VPAT is a blank accessibility report template; a completed one is an Accessibility Conformance Report (ACR).
vpat.why: Buyers, funders, and procurement teams often ask for one.

wcagEm.definition: The official step-by-step method for evaluating a website against WCAG.
wcagEm.why: It is how a credible, repeatable audit is done.

section508.definition: A United States law requiring federal websites to be accessible.

en301549.definition: The European accessibility standard for digital products and services.
en301549.why: It is the EU's equivalent, also based on WCAG.

guideAudit.title: What is an accessibility audit?
guideAudit.description: A plain-language guide to accessibility audits — automated vs manual testing, what a good audit covers, and how to read the result. For NGOs and government.
guideAudit.heading: What is an accessibility audit?
guideAudit.intro: A plain-language guide to checking how accessible a website really is — and what a trustworthy result looks like.
guideAudit.shortBody: An accessibility audit is a structured check of how well a website works for people with disabilities. It measures the site against WCAG (the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) and tells you what passes, what fails, and what needs a closer look.
guideAudit.methodsIntro: No single method catches everything. A credible audit combines both:
guideAudit.automatedWhat: Software assesses the page against rules
guideAudit.aiWhat: AI helps check what automation cannot decide
guideAudit.aiLimit: Not proof — a person still confirms
guideAudit.manualWhat: A person tests with keyboard and screen reader
guideAudit.manualCatches: The rest — usability in real use
guideAudit.coversBody: A credible audit follows a method (WCAG-EM): define the scope, explore the site, choose a representative sample of pages, evaluate them against WCAG, and report the outcome with evidence. The result should say, for each success criterion, whether it passes, fails, is not present, or cannot be decided automatically.
guideAudit.readResultBody: A good report leads with the top issues to fix first — ranked by user impact — with the affected element, the WCAG reference, and a suggested fix. It should also be honest about its limits: an automated score is a starting point, not a certificate of conformance. <link>Read about conformance reports</link>.
guideAudit.q1: Is an automated assessment a full accessibility audit?
guideAudit.a1: No. Automated tools catch roughly 30–50% of issues. A credible audit also needs manual testing and, for some criteria, human judgement — which is why we combine automated assessing, AI-assisted review, and independent human review.
guideAudit.q2: How long does an accessibility audit take?
guideAudit.a2: A single-page automated assessment usually finishes in under a minute. A whole-site assessment takes longer. A full independent audit with human review is scheduled per page.
guideAudit.q3: Do I need to be a developer to run one?
guideAudit.a3: No. You can run a free assessment with just your web address and get a plain-language report. Developers and auditors can go deeper with the evidence and WCAG references.

guideConformance.title: What is a WCAG conformance report?
guideConformance.description: A plain-language guide to WCAG conformance reports — what they contain, what 'passes / fails / needs review' means, and how to use them. For NGOs and government.
guideConformance.heading: What is a WCAG conformance report?
guideConformance.intro: A plain-language guide to the document that shows, with evidence, how accessible a website is.
guideConformance.shortBody: A WCAG conformance report is the record of an accessibility evaluation. It states which standard and level were tested (for example, WCAG 2.2 AA), and for each success criterion whether the site passes, fails, is not present, or needs human review — with the evidence to back it up.
guideConformance.item2Body: pass, fail, not present, or needs review, for every success criterion.
guideConformance.item3Body: machine, AI, or human review, so you can judge the confidence.
guideConformance.item4Body: the top issues to fix first, with evidence and a suggested fix.
guideConformance.item5Body: so the report is an auditable record, not a one-off screenshot.
guideConformance.passesBody: A clean report is not the same as a conformant site. Automated tools only check part of WCAG, so an honest report separates what the machine decided from what still needs a person. That honesty is exactly what makes a report defensible — it shows you investigated rather than assumed. <link>Read about audits</link>.
guideConformance.q1: Does a good score mean my site is compliant?
guideConformance.a1: Not on its own. An automated score covers only part of WCAG. A signed conformance report that includes independent human review (launching soon) is stronger evidence — but even that is a professional opinion, not a legal guarantee.
guideConformance.a2: Some criteria cannot be decided by a machine — for example, whether alt text is accurate, or whether content is genuinely understandable. Those need a person to judge them, which is why our report separates 'machine', 'AI', and 'human' results.
guideConformance.q3: Who asks for a conformance report?
guideConformance.a3: Auditors, ombudsmen, procurement teams, funders, and grant assessors — anyone who needs verifiable evidence rather than a self-declared claim.

guideVpat.title: VPAT and ACR: third-party verification explained
guideVpat.description: A plain-language guide to VPATs and Accessibility Conformance Reports — what they are, why independent verification matters, and how to get one. For NGOs and government.
guideVpat.heading: VPAT and ACR: third-party verification explained
guideVpat.intro: A plain-language guide to the documents procurement teams ask for — and why independent verification carries more weight than a self-declared claim.
guideVpat.shortBody: A <vpat>VPAT</vpat> (Voluntary Product Accessibility Template) is a standard blank template for reporting how accessible a product is. A completed, product-specific VPAT is an <acr>ACR</acr> (Accessibility Conformance Report). When a buyer asks for “a VPAT”, they usually mean the finished ACR — the evidence-backed report, not the empty form.
guideVpat.includes1: The standard and level tested (for example, WCAG 2.2 AA).
guideVpat.includes2: Per-criterion results with evidence — pass, fail, or needs review.
guideVpat.includes3: How each was tested — machine, AI, or human review.
guideVpat.includes4: A signature and date, so it is an auditable record.
guideVpat.q1: Is a VPAT the same as an ACR?
guideVpat.a1: A VPAT is the blank template; a completed, product-specific VPAT is an Accessibility Conformance Report (ACR). Buyers and procurement teams usually ask for the ACR — the filled-in, evidence-backed report.
guideVpat.a2: Anyone can write a self-declared conformance claim. Independent verification — by reviewers with lived experience of disability, outside your team — is what makes the claim credible to procurement, auditors, and funders. Our human-review service is launching soon.
guideVpat.q3: Do I need a VPAT for a government contract?
guideVpat.a3: Often, yes. Public-sector procurement increasingly asks for an ACR (a completed VPAT) as evidence of accessibility. Our signed, dated conformance report — plus independent human review once it launches — supports exactly that.

guideEsg.title: Digital accessibility and ESG reporting
guideEsg.description: How digital accessibility maps to the 'S' in ESG — GRI, ESRS, and SASB — and how to evidence it for funders, investors, and sustainability reports. Plain-language guide.
guideEsg.heading: Digital accessibility and ESG reporting
guideEsg.intro: A plain-language guide to treating accessibility as measurable ESG data — not just a compliance checkbox.
guideEsg.sBody: ESG breaks into Environmental, Social, and Governance. Digital accessibility sits squarely in the <social>Social</social> pillar: it is a measurable form of inclusion — whether your website and digital services exclude people with disabilities. For NGOs, funders, and sustainability teams, that makes accessibility a reportable social outcome, not just a technical task.
guideEsg.mapsTitle: How it maps to the frameworks
guideEsg.rowGriWhere: Social disclosures on inclusion and non-discrimination.
guideEsg.rowEsrsWhere: S1 (own workforce) and affected-communities disclosures on inclusion.
guideEsg.rowSasbWhere: Industry-specific social metrics, including customer/accessibility items.
guideEsg.mapsLink: See how our report maps to GRI, ESRS, and SASB
guideEsg.evidenceBody: A statement that “we care about inclusion” is hard to audit. A signed, dated accessibility conformance report — your score, per-criterion results, and how each was tested — is a concrete data point you can put in an ESG or sustainability report. It turns a value into a verifiable metric. <link>Read about conformance reports</link>.
guideEsg.q1: Which part of ESG does accessibility belong to?
guideEsg.a1: The 'S' — Social. Digital accessibility is a measurable form of social inclusion: whether your digital services exclude people with disabilities. It fits naturally alongside labour practices, human rights, and community impact.
guideEsg.a2: GRI (social/disclosures on inclusion), ESRS (the European Sustainability Reporting Standards, especially S1 own workforce and S2/S3 affected communities), and SASB (industry-specific social metrics). A conformance report gives you concrete, auditable data for these.
guideEsg.q3: What evidence do I actually report?
guideEsg.a3: A signed, dated accessibility conformance report — your score, per-criterion results, and how each was tested — is a concrete, auditable data point for the 'S' disclosure, far stronger than a statement of intention.

a11yStatement.title: Accessibility statement
a11yStatement.description: Ascent Accessibility's commitment to accessibility — the standard we design to, and how to report a problem.
a11yStatement.heading: Accessibility statement
a11yStatement.intro: Ascent Partners Foundation is committed to making this site usable by everyone. We design it alongside screen-reader and keyboard users, not as an afterthought.
a11yStatement.targetBody: We aim for WCAG 2.2 AAA — a stricter standard than the AA level the assessment tool defaults to. The interface uses a high-contrast monospace theme, a single ordered heading outline, standard landmarks, a skip link, visible focus, labeled form fields, and live announcements for dynamic changes. You can adjust text size from the header.
a11yStatement.limitsBody: The embedded payment form is provided by Stripe, whose accessibility is outside our direct control. Our navigation links use a 24px minimum target size with generous spacing (an AA-compliant choice, rather than the full 44px AAA target). If you encounter a barrier on any part of the site, please tell us — we treat accessibility reports as a priority.
a11yStatement.reportBody: Email <mail>contact@ascent-partners.com</mail> and describe what you were trying to do and what happened. We aim to respond within a few business days.

esg.title: Accessibility for business
esg.description: How the Ascent Accessibility conformance evaluation report provides evidence aligned to GRI, ESRS, SASB, Disability:IN, and regulatory accessibility obligations.
esg.heading: Accessibility for business
esg.intro: The "S" in ESG is the question every business now has to answer: what is it actually worth? Digital accessibility is one answer you can measure. The report this tool produces maps your web accessibility to GRI, ESRS, SASB, and Disability:IN — evidence, not intention. And because the engine is open source, the evidence is verifiable.
esg.footer: See how the tool evaluates a site in <link1>our methodology</link1>, or the technical basis in <link2>how we validate the engine</link2>.

compliance.title: Compliance
compliance.description: How WCAG conformance maps to accessibility regulations and standards — EN 301 549, Section 508, the European Accessibility Act, AODA, and BITV.
compliance.heading: Compliance
compliance.intro: WCAG is the technical spine of the world's accessibility laws. Meet WCAG 2.2 AA and you satisfy the WCAG requirements behind most of them — from America's Section 508 to Europe's EN 301 549 and the European Accessibility Act. This page maps the landscape. It is information, not legal advice.

validationPage.title: How we validate the engine
validationPage.description: How the Ascent Accessibility engine is validated — rule-to-criterion coverage, W3C ACT-rules alignment, and test coverage.
validationPage.heading: How we validate the engine
validationPage.intro: Every success criterion is classified by how it is tested — machine-testable, AI-detectable, or manual-only — and the engine links each automated rule to a specific WCAG criterion. The rule catalogue is decomposed into atomic, independently testable checks aligned to the W3C ACT-rules format. The engine is open source (github.com/humanity4ai/ascent-accessibility), so every rule is inspectable.
validationPage.coverageBody: Three layers cover 100% of success criteria: the clean-room rule engine (machine-testable), an AI-assisted review with a confidence fail-safe (AI-detectable), and independent human review by people with lived experience (manual-only — launching soon). No criterion is left unclassified.
validationPage.note: Feature comparison reflects public documentation at the time of writing. The ~30–50% figure is the documented automated-testing ceiling for WCAG, not a criticism of any tool.

remediation.title: Remediation library
remediation.description: Plain-language fixes for every WCAG success criterion — what to change and how to confirm it is resolved.
remediation.heading: Remediation library
remediation.intro: Every failure has a fix. This library explains, in plain language, what to change for each WCAG success criterion — and how to confirm it's resolved. It is the same guidance the tool attaches to every finding it reports.
